record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: What spatially resolved particle-scale scenario governs the shear-induced yielding transition in colloidal or particulate gels, and which clearly defined microscopic and mesoscopic observables from fast confocal microscopy or rheo-tomography can be compared directly with simulations to produce a consistent description of yielding across length scales?

evidence.quote: A long discussion pointed out that we still need to understand the spatially-resolved scenario of the shear-induced yielding transition in gels at the particle scale.

These experiments should primarily concentrate on identifying clearly defined microscale and mesoscale observables, which can be compared with the outcomes of numerical simulations. This comparative analysis aims to offer a consistent description of yielding across a broad range of length scales.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a colloidal or particulate gel: a soft amorphous solid formed by an arrested, percolating network of attractive Brownian particles suspended in a viscous fluid. When subjected to an applied shear deformation (either steady shear at rate γ̇ or oscillatory shear of amplitude γ₀ and frequency ω), such a gel undergoes a yielding transition from a solid-like response to a flowing or fluidized state.

Provide a spatially resolved, particle-scale description of the shear-induced yielding transition in such gels. Specifically:

1. Identify the microscopic mechanism(s) at the level of individual particles and interparticle bonds (e.g., bond breaking and reformation, cage rearrangements, plastic events, non-affine displacements) and the mesoscopic mechanism(s) at the level of network strands, clusters, or force chains (e.g., strand stretching/buckling, cluster rotation, shear-band nucleation, percolation loss) that together govern yielding.

2. Define a set of clearly specified microscale and mesoscale observables — for instance: bond lifetime distributions, coordination number statistics, the non-affine displacement field D²_min, local stress and force-chain network statistics, four-point dynamic susceptibility χ₄(t), spatial correlations of plastic rearrangements, cluster size distributions, and strand-level strain — that
   (a) can be measured experimentally by fast 3D confocal microscopy and rheo-tomography on model colloidal gels under shear, and
   (b) can be computed from particle-based numerical simulations (e.g., Brownian or molecular dynamics of attractive colloids).

3. Show that the proposed observables, when compared between experiment and simulation across the relevant range of length scales (from single-particle to network-spanning), yield a single consistent description of the yielding transition in particulate gels.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent reviews and research on yielding in colloidal and particulate gels (2023–2025) continue to highlight the lack of a unified, spatially resolved particle-scale picture of the yielding transition. While progress has been made identifying ingredients such as bond breaking, non-affine rearrangements, strand stretching and shear-band formation, a single consistent multi-scale description matching confocal/rheo-tomography observables with simulations remains an explicitly open challenge.

status_evidence.title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials
status_evidence.snippet: open questions on yielding in soft amorphous materials
status_evidence.claim: The community frames the spatially resolved particle-scale scenario of gel yielding as an unresolved open question.

status_evidence.title: Yielding and rheology of colloidal gels (recent reviews)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews of colloidal gel yielding emphasize that linking micro/meso observables to a unified yielding picture is still ongoing.
status_evidence.claim: No consensus particle-scale scenario for gel yielding exists as of 2024–2025.
